en: The *Rādhā-kṛṣṇārcana-dīpikā* [was composed by] that venerable Sanātana, who was equal to and senior to Sanātana [Gosvāmī].
That younger brother was Śrī Vallabha, who is Śrī Rūpa, the true refuge of all living beings. //1//
[Note: This verse is also used by Jīva as a maṅgalācaraṇa in other works.
Endowed with the Purāṇas, Saṃhitās, Tantras, Mantras, and Śrutis.
May the scripture of the Gītā and Bhāgavatam be victorious in the abodes of Vraja! //2//
The worship of Śrī Dāmodara and Rādhā is worthy of the inhabitants of Vraja; for this is the indispensable and unsurpassed adoration of the presiding deity of that place. //3//
In this regard, some do not accept that the scriptures are a valid means of knowledge; to them we say:
Lakṣmī is the most feminine of all women, and the Gopīs are renowned as being the most Lakṣmī-like.
If Rādhā is the most beloved of the gopīs, what other beautiful woman could be her equal? //4// Thus it is said.
[*NOTE: This verse is quoted at Gopāla-campū 1.25.

Let it suffice for now that her status as the foremost among the hosts of gopīs, due to her qualities which surpass even those of Lakṣmī, has been established in the Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-sandarbha and other works.
[*NOTE: Portions of the RKAD have been lifted wholesale from the Sandarbhas.]
And here, she who is to be determined as the very form of Lakṣmī of the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Himself is Śrī Rādhā.
Listen to the scriptures regarding how He is worshipped accompanied by the multitude of gopīs alone;
therein, it is shown according to the sequence of ascending stages.
For just as the propitiation of Kṛṣṇa is necessary,
so too is that of His devotees.
If there is no fault, it is difficult to overcome. //5//
[*NOTE: This verse is identical to LBhāg 2.1, except that "mukundasya" is substituted for "hi kṛṣṇasya. The subsequent section follows closely upon LBhāg 2.]
(End of page 1) Herein, regarding Śrī Kṛṣṇa, as it is said in the Gautamīya-tantra:
"In this essence-less and terrible saṃsāra..."
The essence is the worship of the feet of Kṛṣṇa,
having attained birth among humans with pure parents.
Who indeed is more sinful than he who, though being capable, does not offer worship? //6//
In the Mahābhārata:
[He who] protects like a mother,
the creator of the world and its cycles of existence.
One who does not worship the Lord of Gods, one should know him to be a slayer of a Brahmin. //7//
Now, regarding his [disciples], as stated in the Padma Purāṇa:
Mārkaṇḍeya, Ambarīṣa, Vasu, Vyāsa, and Vibhīṣaṇa.
Puṇḍarīka, Bali, Śambhu, Prahlāda, Vidura, and Dhruva. //8//
Dālbhya, Parāśara, Bhīṣma, Nārada, and others— along with the Vaiṣṇavas—
I shall serve Hari, who is to be served by them.
If there were no other fault. //9//
Likewise, in the *Haribhaktisudhodaya* (16.76): "But those who, having worshiped Govinda, do not worship His devotees..."
Those hypocritical people are not recipients of Viṣṇu’s grace. //10//
In the Pādmottara-khaṇḍa:
"Of all forms of worship, the worship of Viṣṇu is supreme."
Therefore, O Goddess, the worship of those [deities] is even more supreme than that. //11//
But he who, having worshipped Govinda, does not worship His devotees, should not be known as a Bhāgavata.
"He alone is considered a hypocrite" (12).
Here and in the preceding passage, by the word "his" (*tadīya*), only his devotees are meant. But others say—(end of page 2)
In this world, there are two types of created beings:
the divine and the demonic.
One who is devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu is divine.
The demonic is the opposite of that. //13//
Thus, according to the rules established in the Viṣṇudharma, Agni Purāṇa, and other texts,
even though He is engaged in the divine play (līlā) of creation and so forth, His state of indifference is appropriate toward those who are indifferent to Him,
and His state of being an object of hatred is appropriate toward those who hate Him.

This has been demonstrated in the same way in the seventh [chapter], at the commencement of the Rājasūya sacrifice, by Śrī Yudhiṣṭhira and others through the hurling of insults and so forth toward Śiśupāla.
Therefore, the Blessed Lord also spoke, beginning with: "Both engagement and withdrawal... (Gītā 16.7).
Those hateful and cruel ones, the lowest of men, who are inauspicious, I perpetually hurl into demonic wombs alone within the cycles of worldly existence. //13//
Having entered the womb of an asura, these deluded ones, failing to reach Me birth after birth, O son of Kuntī, thereafter go to the lowest state. (Gītā 16.19–20) Likewise—
Fools disregard me when I have assumed a human form, being unaware of my supreme nature as the Great Lord of all beings. 15.
"Those whose hopes are vain, whose actions are vain, whose knowledge is vain, and who are devoid of discernment, have resorted to a delusive nature that is both demonic and asuric. (Gītā 9.11–12).
By this, His own devotees are praised.
But the high-souled ones, O Pārtha, having taken refuge in the divine nature, worship me with undistracted minds, knowing me as the imperishable source of all beings. 17.
Constantly glorifying me, striving with firm resolve, and bowing down to me with devotion, they worship me, ever-disciplined. (Gītā 9.13–14)
Therefore, in the eleventh [chapter], it is stated that "the worship of My devotees is superior.
The meaning is that even compared to My own worship, it is superior (*abhi*)—that is, in every respect (*sarvataḥ*)—and it produces greater love for Me.
Thus, it being established that the worship of My devotees is both necessary and internal (*antaraṅga*).
Among all of these as well,
Prahlāda is considered the most excellent.
The greatness of that which has been described [in the Skanda, Bhāgavata, and other Purāṇas] concludes here:
indeed, among all devotees of Hari, Prahlāda is the greatest. //20//
[Note: (SkandaP) LBhāg 2.9] In the seventh [chapter], there is indeed the speech of Prahlāda himself:
"O Lord, where am I, born of rajas, in this world where tamas predominates?"
Born as you are in the lineage of the Asuras, where is your compassion?
It is neither that of Brahmā, nor of Śiva, nor indeed of Lakṣmī, since this gracious favor of placing your lotus-hand upon my head has been bestowed upon me.
In that very context, the speech of Śrī Nṛsiṃha is as follows: "There will be men in the world who are my devotees and devoted to you."
Indeed, you are the embodiment of all my devotees. //22//
The best of the Pāṇḍavas, even more than such as Prahlāda and others, clearly perceive the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam as the perfect authority in every respect. 23.

The experience of the bliss of liberation and nirvana—
younger brother Mātuleya is indeed dear to you, a well-wisher, worthy of self-honor, the performer of rites, and a guru. (7.10.49)
He whose form has not been described by those such as Bhava and Padmaja as a real entity through their intellect,
but who has been worshipped with silence, devotion, and tranquility—

"May this Lord of the Sātvatas be gracious. Śrī-Svāmī-Caraṇa has explained: To the king who was despondent, thinking, "Prahlāda’s fortune is such that he beheld the Lord, whereas we are of meager fortune," [the Lord] spoke with three verses beginning with "You... (yūyam).
The intended meaning of these three verses was written by those very [authorities]:
"The Supreme Brahman does not dwell in the houses of Prahlāda,
nor do sages approach his home for the sake of beholding Him."
Nor does he exist in the form of his maternal cousin and so forth, nor is he himself manifest [in that way].
Therefore, the sense is: "You yourselves are even more fortunate than he, even though he is complete. Thus it is said.
Because they were always so closely related and because of their great devotion to Hari,
some among the Yadavas are considered even more excellent than the Pāṇḍavas.
Likewise, in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, Tenth Canto:
"O you who have taken birth here among men, you are truly being fed! For even a single glance at Kṛṣṇa—which is the very vision of the yogīs—is what you are receiving. (10.82.28)
[Association] consists of seeing, touching, being within earshot, conversing, sharing a bed, a seat, or food, as well as sexual union and the offering of funeral cakes.
In whose house Viṣṇu himself resided— the cessation of heaven and liberation for you who were treading the path to hell.

In lying down, sitting, walking, conversing, playing, bathing, eating, and so forth,
they do not recognize the Self that exists within them.
The Vṛṣṇis have their minds fixed on Kṛṣṇa.
Even among the Yadus, this venerable Śrī Uddhava is the most excellent.
[*NOTE: The first two lines follow LBhāg 2.22. Read "sarvebhyaḥ" for "bhagavān."*] He who was the minister, disciple, servant, and great beloved of the Lord of the Yādavas—
From his very childhood, his devotion to Govinda has always been supreme.
[*NOTE: The last two lines are Lbhag 2.25.

he who is five years old with his mother...
When requested for his morning meal,
he did not desire it, performing service for him with the playful innocence of a child. (BhP 3.2.2)
And in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, in the Tenth Canto:
"Uddhava was the foremost counselor of the Vṛṣṇis, the beloved friend of Kṛṣṇa, a direct disciple of Bṛhaspati, and one esteemed for his intelligence. (10.46.33)
The Blessed Lord Hari, the remover of the distress of those who have taken refuge, once took the hand of that most beloved and single-minded devotee with his own hand and said to him:
"In the eleventh [canto] it is said: 'But you are among the Bhāgavatas, and I am [among them]'. (10.46.1–2; 11.16.24)
"Neither Saṅkarṣaṇa, nor Śrī, nor even the Self is as you are.

(end of page 6).

May He remain here, making [us] grasp [this truth].
(BhP 3.4.3) Because He is not afflicted or oppressed by the *guṇas*—namely *sattva* and the others—the meaning is that He has transcended the *guṇas*.
Since He is the Lord (*prabhu*), He is capable of bestowing the savoring of the essence of devotion (*bhakti-rasa*).

Having seen such distress of the cowherd women caused by their absorption in Kṛṣṇa,
Uddhava was supremely pleased.
While offering obeisance, he sang this (BhP 10.47.57).

These cowherd girls on earth, who bear bodies as the ultimate [embodiments], have thus fixed their love upon Govinda, the Self of all;
that which even sages and we ourselves desire out of fear of worldly existence, they now long for.

Uddhava desired these very things; for it is said in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, Tenth Canto:
"O, may I become one who enjoys even the dust of the feet of those women."
In Vṛndāvana, there is something among the shrubs, creepers, and herbs that—
having abandoned its own kin and the path of the noble— makes [even those things] difficult to forsake.
They took refuge in the state of Mukunda, which is sought after by the Vedas.
(BhP 10.47.61) That it is to be sought after by the Vedas alone is stated right there, as follows:
Even his enemies attained that which the sages, joined in firm yoga with their breath, mind, and eyes stilled, worship within their hearts— merely by remembering Him,
whose minds women fix upon His long, serpent-like arms.
"We too are equal to You, possessing an equal vision, for the nectar of Your lotus feet.
(BhP 10.87.23) Here, even though the word "that" (*tat*) occurs within each pair of verses, it is understood separately as two distinct pairs.
Consequently, [the first *tat* refers to: "That which is called Brahman, which the sages worship and which even Your enemies attained through remembrance."
The women—the goddesses of Śrī-Vraja—attained the nectar of Your lotus feet, which consist of the sweetness of love for You.
We too, being equal to them in vision and identical in disposition, have attained equality with them;
the meaning is that, having become gopīs through another manifestation (*vyūha*), we have become the nectar of Your lotus feet.
In this regard, there are statements preceded by their prayers in the *Bṛhad-vāmana-purāṇa*. The word "strī" (woman) here denotes the *gopīs*.

By the phrase "even their enemies attained [liberation] through remembrance," it is shown that they obtained Śrī Kṛṣṇa Himself—who is renowned as the giver of liberation even to the *asuras*—as their sole object of refuge.
For it is well known that they alone worship Him with exclusive passion;
let this matter rest for now, as their supreme distinction even from Lakṣmī— who resides upon the body of Śrī Nārāyaṇa—
has been demonstrated by that very fact of their possessing such unique devotion to Him.
As it says in that very same place—
(end of page 9)—
"This is not a favor from Śrī, for she is intensely devoted to her own limbs."
"Whence could there be other women possessing the fragrance and luster of lotuses like the celestial damsels? (BhP 10.47.60).
By this [verse], it is shown that all women, including Lakṣmī and others, without exception, attain a similarity in characteristics with them; thus they are "distinct" (vilakṣaṇā).

Furthermore, by the word "arose" (*udagāt*), it is indicated that His grace toward them manifested specifically during the occasion of the *rāsa*-dance, rather than having arisen [spontaneously]; therefore, they possess natural love (*svābhāvika-prema*).
They are of the nature of the eternal beloveds of the Supreme Lord, who sports exclusively in Śrī Vṛndāvana, who is complete, and who is distinct from everything else.
Because they have attained the status of being specific forms of Lakṣmī who are distinct from all others,
it follows that the worship of Him together with them is essential.
Thereafter, according to the maxim of "driving in a post," their essential nature is defined for that purpose.
First, in the *Śrī-Bhagavat-sandarbha* [Note: this is the starting point of the *Bhagavat-sandarbha*. The two following verses are quoted in sections 16 and 21]:
Having thoroughly established the Śrī Bhagavān through such passages as "He is called Brahman, Paramātman, and Bhagavān" (BhP 1.2.11), His two-fold power is described:
that which is called *māyā* and that which is known as His own essential nature (*svarūpa-bhūtā*).
In that regard:
"That which would be perceived apart from an object,
yet would not be perceived within itself..."
One should know that to be the illusory power (māyā) of the Self, just as an appearance or just as darkness;
thus [it is said] by this [verse].
"This Māyā of the Blessed One, which effects creation, maintenance, and dissolution, has been described by us as having three aspects. What more do you wish to hear? (BhP 11.3.16).
By this, the power of Māyā is defined.
And therein, its constituent parts have also been shown.
Furthermore, as stated in BhP 6.16.20: "The mind and the sense organs do not touch You, nor do they know You through all [of their functions]," You are the primordial Person,
the manifest Lord.
Beyond primordial nature,
having cast off illusion by means of the power of consciousness,
he abides in the self within the state of absolute liberation.

By this, His inconceivable power, which constitutes His very essence, is shown; and through its various functions, its endless manifestations are displayed—such as Śrī, Puṣṭi, Gīr, Kānti, Kīrti, Tuṣṭi, Ilā, and Jayā—and how many such divisions are there? (BhP 10.39.55)
And that twofold power is shown in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa as follows:
"O Soul of All, that which is Your lower power residing in all beings..."
O Lord of the Gods, salutations to that eternal one who is the locus of all virtues. 45.
It transcends the range of both speech and mind, is without distinction,
and is to be discerned by the knowledge of the wise.
"I revere that supreme Goddess," [as stated] by this [verse] (ViP 1.19.76–77).
In this regard, the first [nature] is to be disregarded by the venerable Vaiṣṇavas like the world itself, for the very state of being a "world" belongs to Him who is composed of that [nature].
The second, however, is to be worshipped by them as the Blessed Lord, for His very state of being the Blessed Lord belongs to Him who is composed of that [nature].
Thus, it is one and the same reality that shines forth both as the constituent part of His essential nature and as His possessing power.

It has already been demonstrated in that very [text] that the state of possessing conscious power (*cic-śakti-mattā*), which is described as being the very nature of that potency, attains the designation "Bhagavat" while shining forth through its predominance. Now,
this section is introduced to show that when it shines forth through the predominance of its aspect as potency (*śaktitva*), it attains the designation "Lakṣmī."

In that regard, since there is but one single essential nature (*svarūpa*), the power (*śakti*) which constitutes that very essence is also one, though it is threefold—arising from consciousness (*citta*), from being (*sattva*), and from bliss (*ānanda*).
As it is stated in the *Viṣṇu-purāṇa*:
In you, who are the locus of all things, the hladinī, sandhinī, and saṃvit energies are one;
yet they become mixed when they produce both bliss and suffering.
"In you, who are devoid of qualities" (ViP 1.12.68);
and this has been explained by the Svāmins as follows:

The continuous, pervasive consciousness is the power of knowledge (*vidyā-śakti*).
It is one, primary, and non-deviating—that is to say, it is your very own essential nature.

That [power] resides perfectly in you alone, who are the ground of all existence because you are the substratum of everything; it does not reside in individual souls (*jīva*). Furthermore, that threefold power consisting of the *guṇas* does not exist in you.
He explains that very [feeling] as "mixed," producing both joy and distress:
that which produces joy arising from mental clarity is *sāttvika*;
that which produces distress in situations such as separation from sense objects is *tāmasa*.
That which is mixed with both [of these] and produced by sense objects is *rājasī*.
The reason for this is stated: "in that which is devoid of the qualities (*guṇas*) such as *sattva*.

the individual soul (jīva) is that same [Lord] enveloped by his own ignorance.

It is true that such a nature is illusory (*māyika*); this has been established in the *Śrī-daśama-ṭippaṇī* titled *Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī* and in the *Kṛṣṇa-sandarbha*, among other works. For fear of prolixity, it is not elaborated upon here.

Now, generally speaking, the beloveds of Śrī Kṛṣṇa are indeed twofold: those who are eternally perfected (nitya-siddha) and those who have attained perfection through spiritual practice (sādhana-siddha). Among these, the eternally perfected ones are as previously described.
And those perfected through spiritual practice (*sādhana-siddha*) are of three kinds:
those born of sages (*ṛṣija*), the *śrutis*, and celestial maidens (*devakanyā*).
Among these, those born of sages are as described in the *Pādmottara-khaṇḍa*:
(End of 23) Formerly, all the great sages dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest, upon seeing Rāma, who was Hari himself there in his beautiful form, desired to eat him. //79//
They all attained the state of womanhood and were born in Gokula;
having obtained Hari through desire, they were thereafter liberated from the ocean of worldly existence.
Nor should it be said that for those born in Gokula, the possession of a mundane body and so forth is impossible;
for the pastimes of the descent (avatāra-līlā) are intermingled with the mundane,
as it is heard that even in the venerable Queen Devakī there was the birth of those known as the six embryos.

The scriptural authorities (*śrutayaḥ*) are heard thus in the *Bṛhad-vāmana-purāṇa* and other texts; for it has been explained accordingly: "We too have our minds attached to the arms of the Lord of Urugā, which are like the coils of a great serpent" (*BhP* 10.87.23). Furthermore, that Gāyatrī was born among them is stated in the *Sṛṣṭi-khaṇḍa* of the *Padma-purāṇa*, where, during the marriage of Gāyatrī—the cowherd girl—to Brahmā, the following words of Śrī Viṣṇu were addressed to the cowherds:
"Having understood this, I have then given this maiden to Viriñca;
and in your lineage, for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods, I shall take an incarnation, and she shall become my beloved. Thus [he spoke].
And as it is said in the *Śrī-daśama*: "May the celestial women come into being for the sake of His pleasure" (BhP 10.1.13).
From this, it is understood that those celestial women exist solely for the enjoyment of those who are dear to Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
therefore, it is stated specifically, "for the sake of His pleasure."
But it is not for the sake of their pleasure;
therefore, their fourfold nature is described in the *Padma Purāṇa*: "The Gopīs are born of sages, born of cowherds, born of the Vedas, and others."
And those celestial maidens, O king of kings, were never human.
(End of page 24) The cowherd girls alone are eternal;
they are by no means human, because of the negation of ordinary humanity.
Therefore, because they are indeed the power of His own essential nature (*svarūpa-śakti*), the Blessed Lord conceived a desire for amorous play with them;
as Śrī Śuka said:
"The Blessed Lord also spent those nights when the jasmine flowers were in full bloom in autumn..."
Having observed them, he set his mind on sporting, resorting to his *yogamāyā*.
By observing those nights as a source of stimulation (*uddīpana*), the greatness of the love for them—those who are by implication the objective supports (*ālambana*)—is demonstrated.

Just as in the passage beginning "And the sages who delight in the Self," where it is said that Hari possesses such qualities, here it is shown that she possesses such qualities that even in him, who is otherwise self-satisfied, a desire for sport arises.
For this very reason, it is shown in the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa* that his youth was also recognized for the sake of worldly convention:
"Honoring that age of youth, Madhusūdana,
whose nature is immeasurable and who has destroyed all enemies, took delight with them during the nights" (ViP 5.13.60).
And in the *Harivaṃśa*:
"Knowing the proper time and honoring his youth, he, who understood the seasons, gathered the young cowherd girls together at night and rejoiced with them" (*Harivaṃśa* 63.18).

Here, the phrase "one who knows the proper time" (*kālavit*) is explained by the words "having observed those nights," and the phrase "he rejoiced with them" is indicated by "he set his mind on sporting.

Thus, the supreme personhood of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is demonstrated through the objects, the time, and the place; therefore, this desire to sport consists solely of that love characterized as the play of His *hlādinī* potency.
But it is not composed of ordinary desire.

This has been clearly stated by Śrī Svāmī as well in the thirty-second [chapter], where he says that Hari’s heart was moistened by the lamentations of separation, and his mind was overwhelmed by the surging waves of the nectar of his own love.
For this very reason, the venerable Lord of Sages demonstrates the necessity of worshipping Him by means of the fruit of hearing about Him.
Whoever, endowed with faith, hears or narrates this playful pastime of Viṣṇu with the women of Vraja, [attains the supreme goal].
"Having attained supreme devotion to the Blessed Lord, the wise man quickly casts off desire, that disease of the heart, in no long time. (BhP 10.33.42).

Here, by the mere hearing or description of the pastimes of Śrī Kṛṣṇa joined with His beloved consorts, even that which is difficult to achieve through many other spiritual practices [is accomplished].

Since it is explicitly clear that supreme devotion arises and the disease of the heart is swiftly removed by its mere emergence, the fact that this is indeed an injunction (*vidhi*) is established by the incitement [to action] through the description of such an excellence of result (*phalātiśaya*),
just as in the case of the statement: "He whose ladle (*juhū*) is made of *parṇa* wood does not hear an evil report."
Nor should it be said that the youngest [servant] lacks the qualification [for service], because he is described as being "steadfast" (*dhīra*).

Furthermore, since the Blessed Lord himself, in the mantra of vision (*darśana-mantra*), does not mention them by another name but rather specifies the particular names of the *vallavīs*, it is thereby made known that their very nature consists of being limbs that characterize Him.
"One should visualize the host of gods outside of this [mandala], along with the gopīs, gopas, and cattle"—thus it is said in the *Kramadīpikā* (3.32).
And in the *Gautamīya-tantra*:
"Dark as a fresh rain-cloud, with eyes like blue lotuses..."
"I revere Kṛṣṇa, the son of the cowherd women, who has taken the form of a cowherd. (85) Thus, at the beginning [of the hymn]:
"By the sweet sounds of the flute placed upon his lovely lips, he repeatedly delights the hearts of the radiant cowherd girls. (86)
He was like a bee drinking the honey from the lotus-faces of the cowherd girls, agitating their minds with his smiling side-long glances;
he was embraced by those whose bodies were blossoming with youth, as they clung closely to one another. (End of page 26) 87–88.
"Surrounded by cowherd women adorned with variegated garments and ornaments"—thus [it is said].

Here, as in Śrī Śuka’s words to Kardama, "O Brahmin, that queen will quickly and passionately enjoy you" (BhP 3.21.28), the phrase "by women of the cowherd caste" is intended. By the use of two present-tense verbs—*kṣobhayantam* (agitating) and *mohayantam* (deluding)—occurring repeatedly, the eternality of the Gopīs and Kṛṣṇa is indicated through the hymn constantly recited by their worshippers.
And in the Sanatkumāra-kalpa: "Surrounded by cowherd women, seated at the foot of the Kalpa-tree," and so forth.

In the Śauri-tantra of the Rudrayāmala: "May He who is surrounded by cowherds, cows, and cowherdesses, whose neck is adorned with the gleaming claws of Ruru deer, protect us for a long time," and so forth. In the Mṛtyusañjīvana-tantra:
"One should remember Kṛṣṇa, the beloved of the cowherd girls, who incessantly enchants thousands of gopīs in the beautiful Vṛndāvana," and so forth;
"possessing the luster of a full-blown blue lotus," and so forth— thus it is stated in the Svāyambhuva Āgama and other scriptures as well.
[Note: *KK 3.82; KṛṣṇaS 106 (p49fn) attributed to the Mṛtyu-sañjaya-tantra. Padyāvalī 46, attributed to Śaradākara.
Again, the opponent said: "Granted, let them be worthy of worship."
However, their names have not been heard of anywhere.
Even so, in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*, in the context of the *Malla-dvādaśī* within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira, it is said:
"O King of kings, learn from me the names of the gopīs according to their prominence."
Gopālī, Pālikā, Dhanyā, Viśākhā who is established in meditation, Rādhā, Anurādhā, Somābhā, Tārakā, and likewise Daśamī. //89//
This Gopālīya [tantra] must surely be the practice of the Gāyatrī as taught in the Padma [Tantra];
it is known by the name Pālikā, with the suffix *kaṇ*,
and likewise as Daśamī— (end of page 27).
That single name is also read at the very end because it is etymologically significant;
or else, the meaning is that even the tenth [name], Tārakā, is likewise [significant].
Thus, in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the *Prahlāda-saṃhitā*, within the *Dvārakā-māhātmya*, during the occasion of Māyā and the departure of Uddhava (12.25–33):
By the words "or characterized by speech" and so forth, these eight are enumerated: Lalitā, Śyāmalā, Dhanyā, Viśākhā, Rādhā, Śaivyā, Padmā, and Bhadrā.

Furthermore, this is because of the renown of the Āgamas that [the forest] is crowded with hundreds of millions of women, and because of the renown of the Blessed Lord that he is the leader of hundreds of groups of women.
Other [examples] from worldly usage and scripture should also be understood.
Now, since their status as hundreds of millions would otherwise be impossible, it is understood that they possess that very great power.
Even there, Rādhā and Candrāvalī are both preeminent in every respect.
In the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*, Candrāvalī herself is indicated by the term "Somābhā" (Moon-like Splendor), due to the predominance of similarity in meaning;
for here her traditional status as a counterpart to Śrī Rādhā shines forth.
And so says the venerable Bilvamaṅgala:
Having arrived from the temple of Rādhā-mohana, he said to Candrāvalī, "O Rādhā, may there be well-being. Hearing his words, Candrāvalī replied:
"O you whose heart is deluded by the well-being of Kaṃsa! Where have you seen Kaṃsa?"
"Where is Rādhā?"—may Hari, abashed and smiling with downcast face, protect you. //90//
Between those two as well, Rādhikā is in every way superior.
This [Lakṣmī] is the very nature of Mahābhāva, preeminent by virtue of her supreme qualities. //91//
As it is stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa* in the words of the Goddess to Dakṣa:
"Rukmiṇī is in Dvāravatī, Rādhā in the Vṛndāvana forest,
Sītā on Citrakūṭa, and Vindhyavāsinī on the Vindhya mountains."
Devakī is in Mathurā, and Parameśvarī is in Pātāla.
And so forth.

(End of page 28) Here, by the mention of Rukmiṇī in close association [with Devakī], it is made known that just as she alone possesses absolute preeminence in Dvārakā, so too does she in Śrī Vṛndāvana.

As for the statement of non-difference between Rukmiṇī, Rādhā, and Devakī—the manifestations of the internal potency (*svarūpa-śakti*)—that is based solely on their commonality as being potencies (*śaktitva*).
Just as there is oneness between the individual soul (jīvātman) and the Supreme Soul (paramātman) due to the equality of their consciousness (cit), so it is here.

Furthermore, just as the mutual splendor of Rukmiṇī and Kṛṣṇa was described by Śrī Śuka in the passage beginning with "She was destined to be his wife" (BhP 10.53.37), in the same way, the splendor of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa is also described by the Śruti in the Ṛk-pariśiṣṭa.
Lord Mādhava was described by Rādhā, and Rādhikā by Mādhava Himself, as they shine among the people;
"vibhrājante" means "they shine intensely," which is the meaning of the Vedic word.
And Her true nature has been shown to Baladeva by Śrī Kṛṣṇa in the Bṛhad-gautamīya:
I am indeed the triad of principles—sattva, tattva, and paratva;
and my beloved Rādhikā is likewise the embodiment of those three principles. 93.
I am indeed beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), and she too is of the form of my own power (śakti).
Assuming a sattvic form, I am the full Brahman, supreme consciousness. //94//
"Requested by Brahmā, I manifest perfectly in age after age, together with you and with her, for the destruction of those who are hostile to the gods.

(95) Here, the meaning is: "I am that triad of principles (*tattva*)—namely, *sattva* as the state of being the effect, *tattva* as the state of being the cause, and *paratva* as the excellence even beyond that. He makes this known in exactly the same way later on as well.
In the context of meditation—
[one should visualize the Goddess] in her non-dual form, with a luster like molten gold,
wearing red garments and adorned with red ornaments. (96) (end of page 29)
One devoted to devotion should worship Śrī Rādhā on the left side;
Rādhikā, the supreme deity, is said to be composed of Kṛṣṇa himself. (97)
She should be meditated upon with hands granting boons and fearlessness, served by all the deities;
she consists of all prosperity, possesses all splendor, and is the supreme enchantress. (98)
In this context, the explicit statement is simply "one should worship. Likewise, further on in the *Mṛtyusañjīvana-tantra*:
"Clad in yellow garments, with her lotus-like hands joined in the gesture of the bamboo flute..."
"Whose heart is illuminated by the Kaustubha gem, adorned with a forest garland,
the Supreme Goddess who dwells upon the couch of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s feet"— and so forth.
For example:

I worship Goddess Rādhā, who consists of all splendor, who rejoices in supreme bliss, who is fond of the festival of the *rāsa* dance, whose very nature is the bliss of Kṛṣṇa, and who is a great ocean of perfect bliss with the form of the nectar of consciousness. //100// Thus.
"Having meditated," and so forth, is stated in the *Sammohana-tantra*: "One should contemplate the goddess Rādhikā, surrounded by cowherds and the community of cowherds," and so on.
Her preeminence is described in the *Ādivārāha-purāṇa*, in the section concerning the circumambulation of Govardhana at her sacred pool (*tat-kuṇḍa*), as follows:
"Having gone to the north of the Gaṅgā, [one reaches] the Lord of Gods, the Wielder of the Discus..."
A great battle then ensued there between him and Ariṣṭa. //101//
Then, having caused Ariṣṭa, who was in the form of a bull, to be slain there by striking him with his heel in a fit of rage, he established a great sacred ford (mahātīrtha). //102//
Having bathed there at that time, joyful after having killed the bull along with the cowherd, he said to Rādhikā, "O blessed lady, how will this turn out? (103)
There, Rādhā embraced Kṛṣṇa, the performer of effortless deeds, and created a holy bathing place nearby known by her own name;
it is celebrated as Rādhā-kuṇḍa, auspicious and the remover of all sins. (End of page 30)
The fruit of bathing in the Rādhā-kuṇḍa is obtained by one who destroys misfortune. //105//
"By means of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices, there is no need for deliberation here;
sins such as the killing of a cow or the killing of a Brahmin are swiftly destroyed.
(106) Thus, although all those [other wives] were present, her superiority was established because her relationship with him was characterized by such love.
Likewise, in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa as cited in the Vrata-ratnākara:
"Even in his childhood, the Blessed Kṛṣṇa assumed a youthful form and took delight in various pastimes with his beloved Rādhā."
Once, on the full moon day of the month of Kārttika, there was a great festival at the house of Nanda;
on that very day, the Blessed Lord went to the house of Rādhā during the night.
And she, being enraged, bound him around the belly with her girdle-string. //108//
Kṛṣṇa, having reported the great festival at his own home, sought to appease his beloved; thereupon, she spoke to him.
And Kṛṣṇa, his heart delighted by his beloveds, said this to them:
"O slender one, that girdle which was placed upon your waist by me—" (110)
“Dāmodara” is my dear name, O fair-faced one;
there is no name in the worlds that brings me greater pleasure than this. (111)
For one born of Prajāpati, this will always bring about every accomplishment;
and having attained rare devotion, such a person is glorified in my world. //112//
O beloved, when I am bound by my mother with cords in a mortar within the womb of this world, then it shall become manifest. //113//
"Whoever worships me according to the prescribed ritual in this month together with you by means of this name-mantra shall obtain all that is desired.

(114) Here too, it should be understood that [the worshipper] is together with his beloved Rādhā; and by the will of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, even in childhood, he manifests fresh youth just like Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself.
"From that time forth, O King, Nanda’s Vraja became possessed of all prosperity; through the residence of Hari and by His own qualities, it became a playground for Lakṣmī. (BhP 10.5.18).
By this [verse], it is stated that their manifestation occurred immediately after the appearance of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
In that regard as well, her preeminence is to be understood as before. Her description by Śrī Śukadeva with such states of being is as follows:
"Having knit a single frown, overwhelmed by the intensity of her love..."
"Looking as if she were striking [her enemies] with the casting of her side-glances, her lips bitten [in anger]" (BhP 10.32.6).
By this [verse], [it is shown that] *ekamukhyā* means "one who is preeminent"; according to Amara, *eka* means "preeminent" (*mukhya*) or "not incomplete" (*akevala*).
Thus, in the *Śrīmad-Gopāla-tapanīya*, she who is renowned as Gāndharvī should be understood as being that very same person.
Because she is understood to be the foremost in all respects through such indicative marks as her primacy,
for this very reason the worship of Dāmodara conjoined with Śrī Rādhā is prescribed for the month of Kārttika.
Furthermore, in the *Kārttika-māhātmya* contained within the dialogue between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā, the mantra for the morning bath resolve (*saṅkalpa*) is as follows:
"O Janārdana, O Lord of Gods, O Dāmodara, I shall perform the morning bath in the month of Kārttika for your pleasure, together with you. (117)

And because in the mantra for the offering of *arghya*, his name is explicitly mentioned, as follows: "O Dāmodara, O slayer of the lord of the Danujas, accept this *arghya* from me according to the rules for the bath performed in the month of Kārttika by one observing the vow. (118)
"O Hari, during the entire month of Kārttika— which is eternal, occasional, and a witherer of sins— I have offered this guest-offering (arghya) at home together with Rādhā.
Because she is mentioned here as being in a state of union (yugmatva), her preeminence is established.
The scriptural statement from the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* regarding the worship of that couple has already been shown.
Likewise, if the *Daśādhyāyī Kārttika-māhātmya* were indeed derived from the *Padma Purāṇa*, then the worship of that couple would certainly be even more manifest therein.
Similarly, in the statement from the *Āgneya Purāṇa* cited in the *Vāsanā-bhāṣya*, its superiority is also established, as follows:
At dawn, the gopīs questioned Uddhava, the follower of Kṛṣṇa, regarding Hari’s playful pastimes—pastimes that were performed there without Rādhikā alone.
Rādhā, however, remained absorbed in his state of being, her latent desires having come to rest. (120) Thus it is said, and so forth.

By the phrase "absorbed in that state" (*tad-bhāva-saṃlīnā*), it is made known that such words as "O bee, O rogue, O friend" and so forth belong to her alone; thus, her preeminence among all the gopīs is demonstrated.
And this is indeed appropriate, for:
Regarding those women who were searching for Śrī Kṛṣṇa, this speech was heard directed toward Him alone:
"Surely the Lord Hari, the Supreme Controller, has been propitiated by her, since Govinda, being pleased with her, left us and led her into private. (BhP 10.30.28)
O friend, has Acyuta come here with his beloved, bringing complete satisfaction to the eyes by displaying his limbs upon her body—
she who is stained with the saffron from her breasts through contact with the body of her lover? May he grant you bliss.
The fragrance of the lotus-garland of the Lord of the Family wafts here;
resting his arm upon the shoulder of his beloved, he holds a lotus.
"O trees, does Rāmānuja, followed here by swarms of bees blinded with intoxication from the *tulasī* flowers, welcome you with affectionate glances as he walks about? (BhP 10.30.12).
What more need be said? Even among the queens of Dvārakā, a desire for her good fortune is heard;
therefore, Śrī Śukadeva also spoke such words to them, saying: "O virtuous lady, we do not desire sovereignty," and so forth, and then they said:
"We desire the glorious dust of His feet, which is the very fortune of Lakṣmī."
To bear upon his head the fragrance rich with the saffron from the breasts of the Wielder of the Mace.
The women of Vraja, the Pulindas, the grasses and creepers,
and the cowherds all longed for the touch of the feet of that Great Soul as he tended the cows.
125 // Thus,
the longing of the women of Vraja and others is shown: "The Pulinda women were filled with the red dye from the lotus feet of the Wide-strider (Urugāya)..."

By this [verse]: "Smearing their faces and breasts with the auspicious saffron that had adorned the bodies of their beloveds— [the saffron] which had become like mere grass compared to the pain of the fever of love caused by the sight of Him— they offered up that very affliction as an oblation" (BhP 10.21.17).

In this context, by the phrase "with the redness of the lotus feet of the Wide-strider" (10.21.17), together with the expression "adorned by the breasts of his beloved," it is understood that the *kuṅkuma* from the beloved's breast had adhered to His feet;
and that beloved was richly perfumed by the fragrance of her breast-*kuṅkuma*.

Thus, by being restated through a singular grammatical ending, it is understood that even among those [goddesses] who describe her, she is distinguished. This is the meaning: regarding Śrī, who is well-known, only the desire for her is heard there.
But there is no such connection;
for from the words of the wives of the Nāgas, "Desiring whom Śrī performed penance as a woman, abandoning her desires and observing vows for a very long time" (BhP 10.16.36),
and from Uddhava’s statement, "She who was indeed worshipped by Śrī, by Brahmā and others whose desires were fulfilled," and so forth (BhP 10.47.62).
Furthermore, there is no connection between Śrī— who is renowned as Rukmiṇī— and those [women],

because they differ in both time and place. Nor is it appropriate for the women of Vraja to have a longing for a connection with Śrī, as stated in the verse beginning, "This is not a limb of Śrī" (10.47.60).
Because even beyond that, she is heard to be supreme;

therefore, in accordance with the established doctrine stated in such passages as "Rukmiṇī is in Dvāravatī, while Rādhā is in the forest of Vṛndāvana," this speech of the goddesses of Vraja is directed specifically toward that Śrī who shines forth, distinguished from all others.
And thus, just as they are objects of longing there, so too are we, the principal queens; furthermore,
it is probable that this meeting occurred during the day itself,
because the Pulindas were wandering in that very place and because the application of saffron paste was still perceived to be moist.
And this union of the two is not merely of the nature of physical enjoyment;
as it says in the context of the *rāsa*:
"The Blessed Lord also spent those nights when the jasmine flowers were blooming in autumn..."
In the verse, "Having seen [him], she set her mind on sporting" (BhP 10.29.1),
a fresh union is clearly implied;
otherwise, the subsequent statement regarding his indifference toward her for the sake of testing her would be rendered inconsistent.
Since this has been described in the *Veṇu-prakaraṇa*, it is understood through its connection with the flute;
this very point is indicated by the term "urugāya" (the one of wide renown).

Therefore, once she had fallen into a swoon due to the exhaustion of her efforts in playing the flute, for the sake of calming that fainting spell, he—with great haste—applied only the sprout of the *Śrī-caraṇa-sañjīvanī* (the life-restoring herb of the Blessed One’s feet) to her perspiring chest, which was already smeared with saffron.
Even while touching the neck and so forth,
he quickly emerged from that [state], having correctly withdrawn [the limbs] without delay; thus it is understood.
He said that some [gopīs] described Kṛṣṇa to their own friends in his absence;
as for those other than them, there is the statement beginning with "pūrṇāḥ pulindyaḥ" (the Pulindas are full [of him]).
Therefore, it was rightly said: "Lakṣmī is surpassed on all sides by women," and so forth.

And she was described in that very same way by Umāpatidhara, the excellent minister of the great king Lakṣmaṇasena and companion of Śrī Jayadeva, as follows: "By one with the movement of vine-like eyebrows, by another with the opening of her eyes, and by another with smiles brightened by moonlight— thus was he respectfully honored on the road."

Victorious are the glances of the Enemy of Kaṃsa, which fell with trembling supplication upon the face of Rādhā—a face possessing the splendor of modesty yet casting aside respect through the slight of pride. //127//
Śrī Jayadeva also said: "Having placed Rādhā in his heart, he abandoned the beauties of Vraja" (GG 3.1),
and likewise, "The mind of the husband is fastened [to her]" (GG 12.14).
For this very reason: "By the mere realization of that supreme power, which is the supreme Śakti and whose nature is Mahāviṣṇu, [one attains] the supreme state of the Supreme Self."
The arrival of the Lord occurs in just a moment, and not otherwise;
for this Śrī Gokuleśvarī alone is the very embodiment of the totality of love.
By this [means], the Primordial God, the Lord of all, is to be known as easily attainable.
Thus, the statement of the *Pañcarātra*, having been established, shines pre-eminently above all; enough, then, with this extensive collection of authoritative citations.
Therefore, among all the cowherd girls (*gopīs*), Rādhikā is the most venerable, as she is declared to be superior to all in the Purāṇas, Āgamas, and other scriptures.

Therefore, it has been rightly said: "The worship of Śrī Dāmodara and Rādhā is worthy of those residing in Vraja," and so forth. Just as Rādhā is [venerated] in Vṛndāvana, so too is Hari in the form of Dāmodara.
And in the scriptures that have been shown, that pair belongs to each respective Lord.
"Lord Mādhava shines with Rādhā, and Rādhikā shines with Mādhava;
thus they shine among the people," so says the *Pariśiṣṭa*.
The Goddess is not without Viṣṇu, nor is Hari without the Lotus-born;
for it is from this [teaching] that the Hayagrīva-pañcarātra has been revealed here.
Therefore, in the practice of the Kārttika vow, you two are regarded as a divine couple named Rādhā and Dāmodara, both by the world and by the scriptures.

What is the use of much talk? Their pair of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) is seen by means of their pair; since this is shown in the scripture, their state as a pair follows by logical implication (kaimutya).
Some worship Umā and Maheśvara, others Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa; let them worship those deities, but we worship Rādhā and Dāmodara.
Thus may this *Śrī-rādhā-kṛṣṇārcana-dīpikā* (The Lamp for the Worship of Śrī Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa), composed by a certain soul dwelling in Śrī Vṛndāvana, attain perpetual radiance.
